items.title: Deriving 6ND
items.prose: Put the steps of the derivation of $C \approx 6ND$ in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.
items.question: Order the steps.

lines.text: Almost every parameter is a weight that each token meets in one matrix product
Each weight costs one multiply and one add, so a forward pass costs about $2N$ per token
The backward pass needs the gradient of the input and of the weight: two products, $4N$
So one training token costs about $6N$
The backward pass costs the same as the forward pass, $2N$
lines.why: It needs two products per weight matrix, one for the input's gradient and one for the weight's, so twice the forward cost.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Build from one weight to one token to all tokens.

byKey.d1: The backward pass does two products per weight, not one.
byKey.left-out: Every line but one belongs; put the left-out one back.

explain.text: Forward $2N$ plus backward $4N$ gives $6N$ per token. Attention adds a term in $T$ that this count leaves out.

items.title: A small model that beats a big one
items.question: Write your answer as you would brief a portfolio manager.

widget.prompt: A start-up says its 7B model "beats a 70B model" on a benchmark, and asks your fund to invest. What do scaling laws, training tokens and contamination tell you to ask before you believe it?
widget.model:
A claim that a 7B model "beats a 70B model" says nothing until we know the benchmark, the tokens and the test set.

**What scaling laws say to expect.** At equal training data, a 70B model should score better: loss falls as a power law in parameters. But size is only one input. A 7B model trained on many more tokens can match a larger model trained on few; Chinchilla showed a 70B model beating the 175B GPT-3 by training on 1.4 trillion tokens instead of 300 billion. So the first question is how many tokens each model saw, and what compute each run used ($6ND$).

**Questions to ask.**
- Which 70B model, trained on how many tokens, and when? An older, under-trained 70B is an easy target.
- How much compute did the 7B use? 7B on 15 trillion tokens is about $6.3 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs, more than a 70B on 1.4 trillion.
- Which benchmark, and is it one benchmark or many? A single benchmark can be gamed by choosing the best of many checkpoints.
- Contamination: were the test questions, or near copies, in the training data? A model that saw the test scores well without the skill (`post-train` L4 treats this in full).
- Error bars: how many questions, and is the gap larger than the standard error?

**What would convince me.** Several held-out benchmarks, a contamination check against the training corpus, the same prompting for both models, error bars, and the training tokens and compute stated. Then "a 7B model trained on more data matches an older 70B" may well be true, and it is what scaling laws predict.

rubric.text: Explains that size alone does not decide: tokens and compute ($6ND$) matter, as Chinchilla against GPT-3 shows
Asks which 70B model, trained on how many tokens
Asks about contamination of the benchmark in the training data
Asks for several benchmarks, the same prompting and error bars
Says what evidence would convince, and that the claim can be true

items.title: Chinchilla on a cluster

items.question: How many days would it take? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the achieved rate, then by 86,400.

explain.text: The achieved rate is $2.88 \times 10^{17}$ FLOP/s, so about 23.7 days.

items.title: Two allocations
items.prose: Kaplan et al. (2020) advised putting most of a larger budget into model size. Hoffmann et al. (2022) advised growing size and data about equally.
items.question: Which model is the clearest evidence for the second view?

options.why: GPT-3 followed the first view: a large model on relatively few tokens.

options.text: The tiny GPT, 18,017 parameters on 2.56M tokens
options.why: At 142 tokens per parameter it is data-heavy, but it compares nothing.
A single model cannot compare allocations.

feedback.correct: About the same compute, 4 times fewer parameters, over 4 times more tokens, and a better model.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which result compared allocations at a fixed budget?

explain.text: Chinchilla and Gopher used about the same compute. Spending it on 4 times more data with a 4 times smaller model gave the better model.
